subject: bm
title: Business Management
assessment: Question paper: 2 hours (90 marks) | Assignment: 30 marks
intro: The Business Management paper rewards **developed points**, not definitions. Every answer should say what the point is **and** why it matters to the business. One-word or undeveloped answers score zero.

topics.title: Role of business in society
topics.rule:
Businesses exist to satisfy **needs and wants** by producing goods and providing services.

Their role in society:
- Create **wealth** and **employment**
- Provide **goods and services** consumers want
- Pay **taxes** that fund public services
- Drive **innovation** and improve living standards
- Provide **choice** through competition

**Sectors of industry:** primary (extracting raw materials), secondary (manufacturing), tertiary (providing services).
topics.example:
**Q: Explain two ways businesses benefit society. (4)**

**Model answer:** Businesses create employment (1), which gives people income to spend and improves their standard of living (2). Businesses also pay taxes such as corporation tax (1), which the government uses to fund public services like the NHS and schools, benefiting everyone (2).
topics.trap: Giving a list of points with no development. **Every mark needs a 'which means that...'** SQA marks are awarded for the *consequence* of the point, not for naming it.

practice.q: Explain one way businesses provide choice to consumers. (2)
practice.a: Competition between businesses means firms offer different products and prices (1). This gives consumers options so they can pick the product best suited to their needs and budget (2).

practice.q: Describe the difference between a need and a want, with an example. (2)
practice.a: A need is essential for survival, e.g. food, shelter, clothing (1). A want is desirable but not essential, e.g. a games console or a takeaway meal (2).

topics.title: Factors of production
topics.rule:
Four factors of production are needed to make goods and services:

- **Land** — natural resources (raw materials, water, minerals)
- **Labour** — the workforce
- **Capital** — machinery, equipment, money invested
- **Enterprise** — the entrepreneur who takes the risk and organises the other three

Rewards: land → rent, labour → wages, capital → interest, enterprise → profit.
topics.example:
A bakery needs:
- **Land:** the plot and flour from wheat
- **Labour:** bakers and counter staff
- **Capital:** industrial ovens, mixers, delivery van
- **Enterprise:** the owner who set it up and takes the financial risk
topics.trap: Confusing **capital** with 'money in the bank' only. In business, capital means the **tools, machinery and equipment** used in production as well as finance. Also leaving out enterprise, which is the factor that organises all the others.

practice.q: State the reward for each factor of production. (4)
practice.a: Land → rent; labour → wages/salaries; capital → interest; enterprise → profit.

practice.q: Explain why enterprise is essential to a new business. (2)
practice.a: An entrepreneur takes the financial risk of starting the business and organises the other factors of production (1). Without someone willing to take that risk and invest, the business would not exist (2).

topics.title: Sectors of industry & economy
topics.rule:
**Sectors of industry:**
- **Primary** — extracting raw materials (farming, mining, fishing)
- **Secondary** — manufacturing and construction (car plants, bakeries)
- **Tertiary** — providing services (retail, banking, hairdressing)

**Sectors of the economy:**
- **Private** — owned by individuals, profit-driven (Tesco)
- **Public** — owned by government, funded by taxes (NHS, schools)
- **Third** — non-profit, aims to help (charities, social enterprises)
topics.example:
**Q: Explain the difference between the private sector and the third sector. (2)**

**Model answer:** The private sector is owned by individuals or shareholders and exists to make a profit for its owners (1). The third sector, such as charities and social enterprises, aims to help a social cause and reinvests any surplus rather than distributing profit to owners (2).
topics.trap: Mixing up **sectors of industry** (primary/secondary/tertiary) with **sectors of the economy** (private/public/third) — they are different classifications. Also, describing the third sector as 'no money involved' — social enterprises can and do make money, they just do not distribute profit to owners.

practice.q: Classify these by sector of industry: a fishing boat, a car factory, a hotel. (3)
practice.a: Fishing boat = primary; car factory = secondary; hotel = tertiary.

practice.q: Explain why the public sector is funded differently from the private sector. (2)
practice.a: The public sector is funded by taxation and government budgets (1) because it provides services for the whole population and is not run to make a profit (2).

topics.title: Stakeholders
topics.rule:
A **stakeholder** is anyone with an interest in a business.

- **Owners/shareholders** — profit, dividends
- **Employees** — pay, job security, working conditions
- **Customers** — quality, price, service
- **Suppliers** — prompt payment, repeat orders
- **Banks** — loan repayment, interest
- **Local community** — jobs, environment, noise
- **Government** — tax revenue, compliance, employment

Stakeholders can **influence** the business and be **impacted** by it.
topics.example:
**Q: Explain the impact on employees if a factory closes. (2)**

**Model answer:** Employees would lose their income and face redundancy (1). This would affect their ability to pay bills and support their families, and finding new work in a small town could be very difficult (2).
topics.trap: Listing stakeholders without saying **how** they are affected. The marks come from the impact, not the label. Also, forgetting that stakeholders can have **conflicting** interests — employees want higher wages while owners want lower costs.

practice.q: Explain how shareholders can influence a business. (2)
practice.a: Shareholders own part of the company and vote on major decisions at general meetings (1). If they are unhappy with performance they can vote out directors or sell their shares, which can lower the share price (2).

practice.q: Describe one conflict between customers and shareholders. (2)
practice.a: Customers want lower prices and higher quality (1), but shareholders want higher profits, which may mean cutting costs or raising prices — the two aims directly conflict (2).

topics.title: Internal & external environments
topics.rule:
**Internal environment** — factors the business controls:
- Finance, employees, current technology, organisational structure, company culture

**External environment** — factors outside the business's control (**PESTEC**):
- **P**olitical — government policy, tax, Brexit
- **E**conomic — interest rates, inflation, exchange rates
- **S**ocial — demographic change, lifestyle trends, ethics
- **T**echnological — automation, e-commerce, AI
- **E**nvironmental — climate, sustainability pressure
- **C**ompetitive — rival businesses, market share
topics.example:
**Q: Explain how an increase in interest rates affects a small business. (2)**

**Model answer:** If interest rates rise, repayments on the business's existing loans increase (1), raising its costs and reducing profit. It also makes new borrowing more expensive and consumers more cautious about spending (2).
topics.trap: Naming PESTEC factors without explaining their **effect on the business**. Also, listing internal factors as external — remember internal means the business controls it directly.

practice.q: Give two political factors affecting a UK retailer. (2)
practice.a: Changes in corporation tax affect profits; changes to import tariffs or trading rules (e.g. post-Brexit) affect the cost of goods brought in from abroad.

practice.q: Explain how a technological change could threaten a business. (2)
practice.a: If competitors adopt new technology such as online ordering, they may offer faster or cheaper service (1). A business that does not keep up loses customers to those competitors (2).

topics.title: The marketing mix
topics.rule:
The **4 Ps** of the marketing mix:

- **Product** — what is sold, its features and quality
- **Price** — how much is charged (and pricing strategy)
- **Place** — where and how it reaches customers (shops, online)
- **Promotion** — how customers are made aware (advertising, offers)

The mix must be **consistent** — a luxury product needs a high price and premium promotion, not a bargain price and a discount flyer.
topics.example:
**Q: Explain how Nokia's failure to adapt its product affected its market share. (2)**

**Model answer:** Nokia did not develop its product quickly enough when touchscreen smartphones arrived (1). Competitors such as Apple offered features customers wanted, so Nokia lost customers and its market share collapsed (2).
topics.trap: Describing the 4 Ps without linking them to the **specific business in the case study**. Also failing to explain how the elements work **together** — examiners often ask for the benefit of an integrated mix.

practice.q: Explain why a consistent marketing mix matters for a premium brand. (2)
practice.a: All four Ps should signal the same quality message (1). A high price, quality product, exclusive place and prestigious promotion together create a premium image — discounting would damage it (2).

practice.q: Describe one benefit of online selling under 'place'. (2)
practice.a: An online store lets a business reach customers far beyond its local area (1), increasing potential sales without the cost of opening physical shops (2).

topics.title: Market research
topics.rule:
**Market research** gathers information about customers, competitors and the market.

**Desk research (secondary)** — data that already exists: internet, newspapers, government reports, sales records. Cheaper and faster, but may be out of date or not specific to the business.

**Field research (primary)** — new data the business collects: surveys, questionnaires, interviews, focus groups, observation, trials. More specific and up to date, but slower and more expensive.

**Quantitative** data = numbers. **Qualitative** data = opinions and feelings.
topics.example:
**Q: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of a questionnaire. (4)**

**Model answer:** A questionnaire can gather information from many people quickly and cheaply (1), giving a statistically useful picture of customer opinion (2). However, people may not answer honestly or may skip questions (1), so results can be inaccurate and the business may make a wrong decision (2).
topics.trap: Saying field research is 'better' without saying why. Also, confusing desk and field — desk = **already exists**, field = **you collect it yourself**.

practice.q: Give two examples of desk research a café could use. (2)
practice.a: Looking at competitors' prices online; reading local council population and spending reports.

practice.q: Explain why a focus group is useful for testing a new product. (2)
practice.a: A focus group gives detailed opinions and lets the business ask follow-up questions (1), so it can understand *why* people like or dislike a product and improve it before launch (2).

topics.title: Market segmentation
topics.rule:
**Segmenting** means dividing a market into groups of customers with similar characteristics, so marketing can be targeted.

Common ways to segment:
- **Age** — children, teenagers, adults, older people
- **Gender** — male/female focused products
- **Income** — budget vs luxury
- **Location** — local, national, rural/urban
- **Lifestyle** — health-conscious, sporty, eco-minded

A **target market** is the segment the business aims its product at.
topics.example:
**Q: Explain how a business could use age to segment a market. (2)**

**Model answer:** The business could identify that teenagers are the main users of its product (1). It could then focus advertising on social media platforms those teenagers use, rather than expensive television advertising (2).
topics.trap: Describing a segment without explaining the **marketing benefit** of targeting it. Also, assuming one segment is the whole market — businesses often target several.

practice.q: Describe two ways a gym could segment its market. (2)
practice.a: By lifestyle — serious athletes versus casual exercisers; by age — students versus older adults wanting low-impact exercise.

practice.q: Explain one benefit of segmentation. (2)
practice.a: Segmenting lets a business direct its marketing effort at the people most likely to buy (1), which means less money wasted on advertising to people who are not interested and more effective sales (2).

topics.title: Product life cycle
topics.rule:
Four stages: **Development → Introduction → Growth → Maturity → Decline**.

- **Introduction:** low sales, high promotion costs, often a loss
- **Growth:** sales rise quickly, competitors enter
- **Maturity:** sales peak, competition fierce, profits squeezed
- **Decline:** sales fall, business must decide to update, discount or withdraw

Strategies to extend the cycle: product development, new markets, rebranding, price cuts.
topics.example:
**Q: Explain the strategy a business might use when a product reaches maturity. (2)**

**Model answer:** When sales peak in maturity, the business might extend the product's life by updating it, for example adding new features or new flavours (1). This can attract existing customers to buy again and delay the decline in sales (2).
topics.trap: Getting the stages **out of order** or confusing maturity with decline — maturity is the **peak**, decline is after it. Also, describing the stages without stating the business action for each.

practice.q: State what happens to profits in the introduction stage and why. (2)
practice.a: Profits are usually negative or low. This is because heavy spending on promotion is needed to make customers aware of the product, but sales volumes are still small.

practice.q: Give two ways a business can extend a product's life cycle. (2)
practice.a: Update or improve the product to attract renewed interest; find new markets or new uses for the product.

topics.title: Branding & promotion
topics.rule:
A **brand** is a name, logo or design that identifies a product and distinguishes it from competitors.

Benefits of branding: customer loyalty, ability to charge a **higher price**, easier product launches, protection from competition.

**Promotion** methods:
- **Advertising** — TV, radio, billboard, online, social media
- **Sales promotion** — discounts, buy-one-get-one-free, competitions, loyalty schemes
- **Personal selling** — shop staff, sales representatives
- **Public relations (PR)** — press releases, sponsorship, social media posts
- **Direct marketing** — emails, texts, mailshots

Choose promotion by **cost**, **target market** and **reach**.
topics.example:
**Q: Explain how a strong brand allows a business to charge higher prices. (2)**

**Model answer:** A trusted brand means customers believe the product is higher quality and are willing to pay more for it (1). It also reduces the risk of switching to an unknown brand, so customers stay loyal even when cheaper alternatives exist (2).
topics.trap: Listing promotion methods without evaluating them in the case-study context. The best answers say **why** a specific method suits that business and its target market.

practice.q: Explain one advantage of social media promotion over television advertising. (2)
practice.a: Social media is far cheaper and lets a business target a specific group by age and interest (1). It can also reach young customers who watch less television, so the money is used more effectively (2).

practice.q: Give two benefits of a loyalty scheme. (2)
practice.a: It encourages repeat custom from existing customers; it builds a database of customer data that can be used for targeted marketing.

topics.title: Pricing & distribution
topics.rule:
**Pricing strategies:**
- **Skimming** — high initial price, lowered later (new technology)
- **Penetration** — low price to win market share quickly
- **Competitive** — match or beat rivals' prices
- **Cost-plus** — cost of production plus a mark-up
- **Premium** — high price to signal quality
- **Loss leader** — sold below cost to attract customers who buy other items

Factors: production costs, competition, target market, economy, brand strength.

**Distribution** is how the product reaches the customer: direct (online/shop), retailer, wholesaler, or agent.
topics.example:
**Q: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of penetration pricing. (4)**

**Model answer:** Penetration pricing sets a low price to attract customers quickly (1), which can build market share and win loyalty before competitors respond (2). However, the low price means low or negative profit margins (1), and customers may see the product as cheap, making it hard to raise the price later (2).
topics.trap: Confusing **skimming** and **penetration** — skimming starts **high** and falls; penetration starts **low**. Also, recommending a pricing strategy without reference to the business's costs or target market.

practice.q: Which pricing strategy suits a brand-new budget phone? Justify. (2)
practice.a: Penetration pricing. It makes the phone attractive to price-sensitive customers, winning market share quickly against established brands.

practice.q: Explain the difference between selling via a wholesaler and selling directly online. (2)
practice.a: A wholesaler buys in bulk and distributes to retailers, so the business loses some profit per unit but reaches many shops. Selling direct online keeps more profit per sale but the business must generate its own customers and handle delivery.

topics.title: Suppliers & supply chain
topics.rule:
Factors when choosing a supplier:
- **Price** — cost of materials
- **Quality** — reliability of the materials
- **Reliability** — consistently delivering on time
- **Delivery** — speed and lead time
- **Payment terms** — credit offered
- **Ethical/environmental** — sustainability record
- **Location** — local suppliers reduce transport costs

A **supply chain** is the whole sequence of organisations involved in getting a product to the customer. Poor supplier choice causes production delays, lost sales and reputational damage.
topics.example:
**Q: Explain the impact on a restaurant of using an unreliable supplier. (2)**

**Model answer:** An unreliable supplier may deliver late or substitute items, so the kitchen cannot produce menu dishes (1). This leads to disappointed customers, lost sales and damage to the restaurant's reputation (2).
topics.trap: Listing criteria without explaining the **consequence** of getting them wrong. Also, forgetting the ethical dimension — SQA rewards answers mentioning fair trade and sustainability.

practice.q: Give two advantages of using a local supplier. (2)
practice.a: Lower transport costs and a faster, shorter delivery time; also better for the local community and the environment.

practice.q: Explain the risk of relying on a single supplier. (2)
practice.a: If that supplier fails, strikes or increases prices, the business has no alternative source (1), so production may stop entirely and the business loses sales (2).

topics.title: Inventory management
topics.rule:
**Inventory** (stock) is the materials and goods a business holds.

Three types:
- **Raw materials** — not yet used
- **Work in progress** — partly made
- **Finished goods** — ready to sell

**Costs of holding stock:** storage, insurance, security, money tied up, risk of damage/obsolescence.

**Costs of too little stock:** lost sales, production stoppages, unhappy customers.

Methods: **JIT (just-in-time)** — order only when needed, reduces storage costs but risks delays. **Buffer stock** — minimum held to cover demand.
topics.example:
**Q: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of holding buffer stock. (4)**

**Model answer:** Buffer stock means the business can keep selling even if a delivery is late or demand suddenly increases (1), so it avoids lost sales and keeps customers happy (2). However, holding extra stock costs money in storage, insurance and security (1), and there is a risk it becomes obsolete or damaged before it is sold (2).
topics.trap: Confusing JIT with 'no stock at all'. JIT means minimal stock, ordered to arrive just as needed. Also, only listing storage costs without mentioning the opposite risk of **lost sales** from too little stock.

practice.q: Name the three types of inventory. (3)
practice.a: Raw materials; work in progress; finished goods.

practice.q: Explain why a bakery might prefer JIT for flour. (2)
practice.a: Flour is bulky and can spoil or attract pests, so holding large amounts is costly and risky. JIT orders frequent smaller deliveries, reducing storage space and waste.

topics.title: Methods of production
topics.rule:
- **Job production** — one bespoke item at a time (a wedding dress, a custom kitchen). High quality, high cost, slow.
- **Batch production** — a group of identical items made together, then the process changes (bakeries, furniture runs). Flexible but requires storage and set-up time.
- **Flow/mass production** — continuous production of identical items on a line (cars, drinks). Cheap per unit but very inflexible and needs high investment.

Choose based on **volume**, **customisation** and **cost**.
topics.example:
**Q: Explain why a furniture maker might use job production. (2)**

**Model answer:** Each piece of furniture can be made to the customer's exact specifications in size, wood and finish (1). This gives high quality and customer satisfaction, which matters more than speed for bespoke products (2).
topics.trap: Saying flow production is 'always best because it is cheapest' — the answer must weigh the **lack of flexibility**. Also confusing batch and flow: batch changes to a different product; flow does not.

practice.q: Which production method suits a company making 2 million identical bottles a day? (1)
practice.a: Flow/mass production.

practice.q: Explain one disadvantage of job production. (2)
practice.a: Each item is made individually, so labour costs per unit are high and production is slow (1), meaning the business cannot easily meet a large sudden increase in demand (2).

topics.title: Quality management
topics.rule:
**Quality control** — checking finished products and rejecting faulty ones. Catches errors **at the end**, which wastes materials.

**Quality assurance** — building quality into every stage of production; checking at each step. Prevents errors rather than catching them.

Benefits of good quality: customer loyalty, fewer returns, premium pricing, good reputation, legal compliance.

Costs of poor quality: recalls, compensation, lost customers, bad publicity.
topics.example:
**Q: Explain the difference between quality control and quality assurance. (2)**

**Model answer:** Quality control checks finished products and rejects those with faults (1). Quality assurance builds checks into every stage of production so faults are prevented before the product is finished (2).
topics.trap: Using the terms interchangeably. Also, only listing benefits without saying **how** the business achieves quality (training, standards, inspection).

practice.q: Give two costs to a business of poor quality. (2)
practice.a: Products must be recalled or replaced, which is expensive; customers lose trust and go to competitors, reducing future sales.

practice.q: Explain how staff training improves quality. (2)
practice.a: Trained staff make fewer mistakes because they understand the standards and correct procedures (1), so less time and material is wasted on faulty work (2).

topics.title: Human resource planning
topics.rule:
**Human resource planning** ensures the business has the right number of staff, with the right skills, at the right time.

Steps: forecast demand → audit current staff → identify gaps → recruit/train/redeploy → review.

**Workforce planning issues:** staff turnover, absence, ageing workforce, skills shortages, seasonal demand.

**Flexible working:** part-time, job share, zero-hours, temporary contracts — reduces fixed costs but can reduce loyalty.
topics.example:
**Q: Explain why a hotel might use part-time staff. (2)**

**Model answer:** Demand varies, with busy weekends and quiet weekdays (1), so part-time staff let the hotel match staffing to demand and avoid paying for idle hours (2).
topics.trap: Confusing HR planning with recruitment — planning comes **first**, and decides whether recruitment is even needed. Also, assuming part-time staff are always cheaper; training costs per head may rise.

practice.q: State two consequences of high staff turnover. (2)
practice.a: Increased recruitment and training costs; loss of experienced staff and reduced service quality.

practice.q: Explain one benefit of flexible working to an employee. (2)
practice.a: It allows them to fit work around family or study commitments (1), which improves work-life balance and can make them more motivated (2).

topics.title: Recruitment & selection
topics.rule:
**Recruitment** = attracting candidates. **Selection** = choosing the best one.

**Internal recruitment** — promote from within. Cheaper, faster, motivates staff; but brings no new ideas and leaves a gap.

**External recruitment** — advertise outside. Brings fresh skills and ideas; but costs more and takes longer.

**Selection methods:** application forms, CVs, interviews, testing, assessment centres, references.

Steps: job analysis → job description → person specification → advertise → shortlist → interview → select → contract.
topics.example:
**Q: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of internal recruitment. (4)**

**Model answer:** Internal recruitment is cheaper and quicker because the business already knows the candidate's abilities and does not need to advertise widely (1); it also motivates staff by showing promotion is possible (2). However, it brings no new ideas or experience into the business (1), and it leaves a vacancy in the employee's old job that must still be filled (2).
topics.trap: Confusing the **job description** (what the job involves) with the **person specification** (the qualities the person needs). Also, listing recruitment methods without explaining their suitability.

practice.q: Explain the difference between a job description and a person specification. (2)
practice.a: A job description lists the duties and responsibilities of the post. A person specification lists the qualifications, skills and qualities the ideal candidate should have.

practice.q: Give two advantages of using interviews to select staff. (2)
practice.a: They let the employer meet candidates and assess personality and communication; they allow questions to be explored in depth.

topics.title: Training
topics.rule:
**Induction training** — introduces new staff to the business, its policies, safety and colleagues. Reduces early mistakes.

**On-the-job training** — learning while doing the job, often from a mentor. Realistic and cheap, but can pass on bad habits.

**Off-the-job training** — at a college or training centre. Expert teaching and no production disruption, but expensive and the skills may not transfer directly.

Benefits: better quality, fewer accidents, higher motivation, legal compliance. Costs: money, lost production time, staff may leave after training.
topics.example:
**Q: Explain why a construction firm uses on-the-job training. (2)**

**Model answer:** Trainees learn practical skills on real sites with actual tools and materials (1), so they develop the exact techniques the firm needs while still contributing to work (2).
topics.trap: Saying training is 'good' without naming the type and its specific benefit/cost. Also forgetting that **off-the-job** training removes staff from production, which is a cost.

practice.q: State two benefits of induction training. (2)
practice.a: New staff learn health and safety rules, reducing accidents; they understand policies and settle in faster, reducing early mistakes.

practice.q: Explain one disadvantage of off-the-job training. (2)
practice.a: It is expensive to pay for courses and the employee's wages while they are absent (1), and the business loses their productive output during that time (2).

topics.title: Motivation
topics.rule:
**Financial motivators:** wages/salaries, bonus, commission, piece rate, profit sharing, overtime, fringe benefits (company car, discounts).

**Non-financial motivators:** job rotation, job enrichment, autonomy, praise, promotion prospects, good working conditions, team working.

**Theories to name:**
- **Maslow** — needs from basic (pay, safety) to higher (belonging, esteem, self-actualisation)
- **Herzberg** — hygiene factors (pay, conditions) prevent dissatisfaction; motivators (achievement, responsibility) create satisfaction

A motivated workforce: higher productivity, lower turnover, better quality.
topics.example:
**Q: Explain how a bonus scheme could motivate staff. (2)**

**Model answer:** A bonus rewards staff financially for hitting a target (1), which gives them a direct reason to work harder and increase output or quality (2).
topics.trap: Describing a motivator without explaining **why it motivates**. Also, assuming money motivates everyone equally — non-financial motivators matter for many staff, and Herzberg argues pay only prevents dissatisfaction.

practice.q: Explain the difference between job rotation and job enrichment. (2)
practice.a: Job rotation moves staff between different tasks to add variety. Job enrichment gives staff more responsibility and autonomy within their role.

practice.q: Give two non-financial motivators. (2)
practice.a: Praise and recognition; opportunities for promotion or greater responsibility.

topics.title: Sources of finance
topics.rule:
**Internal sources** (from inside the business):
- Retained profit, sale of assets, owner's capital, working capital

**External sources** (from outside):
- **Short term:** bank overdraft, trade credit
- **Medium term:** bank loan, leasing, hire purchase
- **Long term:** mortgage, share issue, debenture, grant, crowdfunding

Choose by **amount needed**, **time period**, **cost**, and whether the business wants to give away ownership.
topics.example:
**Q: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of a bank loan. (4)**

**Model answer:** A bank loan provides a large sum immediately (1) and can be repaid in fixed instalments, making budgeting easier (2). However, the business must pay interest, which increases the total cost (1), and the bank may refuse if the business has a poor credit record or require security (2).
topics.trap: Confusing **overdraft** (short-term, flexible, expensive) with a **loan** (fixed sum, longer term). Also, recommending share issue for a small business — it gives away ownership and control, which most owners resist.

practice.q: Which source suits a business needing cash for two weeks until customers pay? (1)
practice.a: A bank overdraft — short term and flexible.

practice.q: Explain one advantage of retained profit as a source of finance. (2)
practice.a: It costs nothing in interest or fees and does not require the owner to give up any control or ownership (1), so all future profit stays with the business (2).

topics.title: Break-even
topics.rule:
**Break-even** is the level of sales where total revenue equals total costs — no profit, no loss.

**Break-even quantity** $=\dfrac{\text{fixed costs}}{\text{selling price} - \text{variable cost per unit}}$

- **Fixed costs** do not change with output (rent, insurance)
- **Variable costs** change with output (materials, packaging)
- **Contribution per unit** = selling price − variable cost per unit

**Margin of safety** = actual sales − break-even sales.
topics.example:
Fixed costs £6,000. Selling price £20. Variable cost per unit £8.

Contribution per unit $=20-8=\pounds12$

Break-even $=\dfrac{6000}{12}=500$ units

If the business sells 650 units: margin of safety $=650-500=150$ units.
topics.trap: Subtracting variable cost from fixed cost instead of from the **selling price**. Also, forgetting that break-even is measured in **units**, not money. A lower break-even point is generally better — it means less risk.

practice.q: Fixed costs £4,500; price £15; variable cost £6. Calculate break-even.
practice.a: Contribution $=15-6=\pounds9$. Break-even $=\dfrac{4500}{9}=500$ units.

practice.q: Using the same figures, calculate the margin of safety at sales of 620 units.

topics.title: Cash flow forecasting
topics.rule:
A **cash flow forecast** predicts money coming in and going out over a period.

Key terms:
- **Inflows** — money received (sales, loans, investment)
- **Outflows** — money paid (wages, materials, rent)
- **Net cash flow** = inflows − outflows
- **Opening balance** — cash at the start of the month
- **Closing balance** = opening balance + net cash flow

The closing balance becomes the **next month's opening balance**.
topics.example:
Opening balance £2,000. Inflows £5,000. Outflows £6,500.

Net cash flow $=5{,}000-6{,}500=-\pounds1{,}500$

Closing balance $=2{,}000+(-1{,}500)=\pounds500$
topics.trap: Forgetting to carry the closing balance forward as the next opening balance — this causes the whole forecast to be wrong. Also, a **negative closing balance** is not automatically failure, but it does mean the business needs additional finance.

practice.q: Opening balance £800; inflows £2,400; outflows £3,600. Find the closing balance.
practice.a: Net $=2400-3600=-\pounds1{,}200$. Closing $=800-1200=-\pounds400$ (an overdraft position).

practice.q: Why might a profitable business still run out of cash?
practice.a: Profit is recorded when a sale is made, but cash arrives later if customers buy on credit. If outflows such as wages and rent fall due before the cash is received, the business can run out of cash despite being profitable.

topics.title: Income statement
topics.rule:
The **income statement** (trading, profit and loss account) calculates profit over a period.

$$\text{Gross profit} = \text{Sales revenue} - \text{Cost of goods sold}$$

$$\text{Net profit} = \text{Gross profit} - \text{Expenses}$$

- **Cost of goods sold** = opening stock + purchases − closing stock
- **Expenses** are overheads: rent, wages, insurance, advertising

Gross profit margin $=\dfrac{\text{gross profit}}{\text{sales}}\times100$
topics.trap: Confusing **gross** and **net** profit. Gross is after cost of goods sold only; net is after **all** expenses. Also, mixing up purchases with cost of goods sold — you must adjust for stock.

practice.q: Sales £50,000; COGS £30,000; expenses £12,000. Calculate gross and net profit.
Calculate the gross profit margin for the figures above.

topics.title: Ratio analysis
topics.rule:
Ratios assess a business's performance and financial position.

**Profitability:**
- Gross profit margin $=\dfrac{\text{gross profit}}{\text{sales}}\times100\%$
- Net profit margin $=\dfrac{\text{net profit}}{\text{sales}}\times100\%$

**Liquidity:**
- Current ratio $=\dfrac{\text{current assets}}{\text{current liabilities}}$ (ideal ≈ 2:1)
- Acid test $=\dfrac{\text{current assets} - \text{stock}}{\text{current liabilities}}$ (ideal ≈ 1:1)

**Efficiency:**
- Rate of stock turnover $=\dfrac{\text{cost of goods sold}}{\text{average stock}}$

Always **compare** — to last year or a rival — and comment on whether the result is good or concerning.
topics.example:
Current assets £60,000 (including stock £20,000). Current liabilities £25,000.

Current ratio $=\dfrac{60{,}000}{25{,}000}=2.4:1$ — healthy liquidity.

Acid test $=\dfrac{60{,}000-20{,}000}{25{,}000}=1.6:1$ — still comfortable.

The business can comfortably pay its short-term debts.
topics.trap: Calculating a ratio but not **commenting** on it — the analysis marks come from interpretation. Also, using the acid test without removing stock from current assets. Higher is not always better: too high a current ratio can mean cash is sitting idle.

practice.q: A business has net profit £15,000 on sales of £120,000. Calculate the net profit margin.
Current assets £40,000, stock £15,000, current liabilities £30,000. Calculate the acid test ratio and comment.
practice.a: $\dfrac{40{,}000-15{,}000}{30{,}000}=\dfrac{25{,}000}{30{,}000}=0.83:1$. This is below the ideal 1:1, suggesting the business may struggle to pay short-term debts without selling stock.
